BDI.story:
Burundi's record on this map concerns abuse committed abroad by its own soldiers on peace missions. Burundian troops served with MINUSCA, the UN peacekeeping mission in the Central African Republic, and with AMISOM, the African Union's mission in Somalia, and in both places they are accused of sexually abusing girls who depended on them. In Dékoa, in the Central African Republic, two allegations against Gabonese and Burundian soldiers led UN investigators to interview some 136 alleged victims, 48 percent of all victims the UN recorded in 2016. UN data list allegations against Burundian personnel involving 46 children between 2014 and 2016. In Mogadishu, Human Rights Watch documented in 2014 rape and sexual exploitation by Ugandan and Burundian soldiers on their bases, including girls under 18. Many of the women and girls had come to the bases for medicine or aid, and some were pressed into sex in exchange for money, food and medicine.

Whether these soldiers face trial is decided in Burundi. Under UN rules only the country that sent the troops can prosecute them; the UN itself can only send them home. Press accounts reported that 41 soldiers identified in the Dékoa case were sent home without charges, and the UN Secretary-General's 2017 report said investigations by the sending countries were still pending. A 2005 report for the Secretary-General had already found that about 45 percent of 105 allegations against peacekeepers in 2004 involved sex with people under 18, and recommended courts martial held where the abuse took place.

What happens to children inside Burundi is barely counted. The US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC), which receives reports of online abuse mostly from US internet companies, logged 1,028 reports for Burundi in 2024, or 7.3 per 100,000 people. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) rates the human trafficking market at 8.5 out of 10 and the role of criminals inside the state at 8.5, with resilience at 2.33. The anti-slavery group Walk Free estimates 89,000 people in modern slavery, counting all ages and all forms.

The records show no charges against the Burundian soldiers accused in the Central African Republic. The map holds no case about children inside Burundi itself.

BLR.story:
The main documented form of child abuse in Belarus is the sale of online access to abuse material, run from Minsk for paying customers abroad. Regpay Co. Ltd, a company in Minsk, processed paid memberships to about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it ran itself, for thousands of subscribers around the world. Buyers paid by credit card. The payments were routed through banks in Latvia, and Connections USA, a payment firm in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, helped launder the money.

The case was investigated and tried outside Belarus. US agents used a ruse to bring Regpay's president Yahor Zalatarou and marketing director Alexei Buchnev to a Paris hotel, where they were arrested on 30 July 2003. Technical administrator Aliaksandr Boika was arrested in Tarragona, Spain, the next day and extradited. All pleaded guilty in New Jersey. Zalatarou and Boika were each sentenced to 25 years in August 2006, and Buchnev to 40 months. The chief executive of Connections pleaded guilty to money laundering, and hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the United States and other countries. The US Attorney General announced the case in January 2004 as part of Operation Falcon.

The volume of online abuse reported today is large. NCMEC, the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, which receives reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 49,821 reports for Belarus in 2024, or 545.5 per 100,000 people. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) rates the role of criminals inside the state at 9 out of 10 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 3.08. The US State Department places Belarus in Tier 3, its lowest rating, given to governments it finds are not making significant efforts against trafficking. Walk Free, an anti-slavery group, estimates 107,000 people in modern slavery, counting all ages and all forms.

Regpay is more than twenty years old and is the only network run from Belarus on the map. No later case on the map explains the current number of reports.

CHN.story:
Two forms dominate China's record, and both involve buying children or girls. One is the sale of babies into state orphanages for adoption abroad. The other is the purchase of girls and women from neighbouring countries as wives for Chinese men.

China opened intercountry adoption in 1992 and sent about 160,000 children abroad. The United States issued 87,704 immigrant visas to children adopted from China between 1994 and 2014; others went to Spain, Canada, Britain, the Netherlands, France and Australia. The New Yorker reported that the programme came to depend more and more on abuse, abduction and trafficking. Between 2002 and 2005, six state orphanages in Hunan province bought infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong province, and placed nearly 1,000 children with families in China and abroad. According to the state news agency Xinhua, 23 civil officials were fired in 2005, three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years and six others to between 3 and 13 years. The programme continued for almost twenty more years. On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry ended it, except for adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

The second form draws on poverty and war across China's borders. Human Rights Watch reported in 2019 that women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan states in Myanmar, many displaced by conflict, were sold to Chinese families for US$3,000 to 13,000, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency listed 629 girls and women sold as brides to Chinese men from 2018 to mid-2019, many from poor Christian communities. Officials told AP the inquiry largely stopped after June 2019 because of pressure from officials worried about relations with Beijing, and in October 2019 a court in Faisalabad acquitted 31 Chinese nationals after witnesses were threatened or bribed. The 2025 US State Department reports describe the same trade from Vietnam, mainly Hmong girls, and from Laos, including forced surrogacy.

Online abuse in China is largely uncounted. NCMEC, the US body that receives reports from mostly US internet companies, logged 9,406 reports for China in 2024, 0.7 per 100,000 people, because US platforms are largely blocked there. The US State Department rates China Tier 3, its lowest grade.

Adoption abroad has ended. The 2025 US reports say the sale of girls from Myanmar, Vietnam and Laos into China continues.

CZE.story:
Most of Czechia's record concerns the making and sale of abuse images of children, and the buying of access to them online. The largest Czech case on the map began with a Czech photographer who, according to Europol, the European Union's police agency, exploited close to 70 children from poor and socially disadvantaged families. With a partner in Sweden he sold the images to customers in the European Union and Canada. Czech police started the investigation, called Operation Atelier, with support from Europol and Eurojust, the EU body that links national prosecutors. In 2014 ten people were arrested and charged: five in Czechia, two in Sweden, and one each in France, Ireland and Spain. Police seized 30 terabytes of data.

Buyers in Czechia also pay for access. Between late May and mid-June 2026, police in Czechia, Canada, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men suspected of paying cryptocurrency to enter dark-web forums holding abuse videos; Norwegian police traced the payments with a method developed in 2025. Czechia was also among the countries in the 2025 operation against Kidflix, a paid streaming site with 1.8 million users, and in Operation Cumberland against a paid site of abuse images made with artificial intelligence, a case in which Europol noted that national laws did not yet cover such material.

In the Catholic Church, the map records one case of an accused priest being moved. Fr František Merta was found guilty in 2000–2001 of abusing more than 20 boys and received a two-year suspended sentence. Archbishop Jan Graubner of Olomouc is alleged to have failed to report him and to have moved him between parishes when problems arose. The map records no national inquiry into church abuse in Czechia.

NCMEC, the US centre that receives online abuse reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 32,140 reports for Czechia in 2024, or 294.7 per 100,000 people. The US State Department rates Czechia Tier 1, meaning it meets the minimum US standards against trafficking.

Czech police have joined the recent European operations against paid abuse sites recorded on the map. How the church handled accused priests across the country has not been examined by any inquiry on record.

ERI.story:
Eritrea appears on this map mainly through its army's conduct in the war in Tigray, the northern region of neighbouring Ethiopia. The International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia, a UN-appointed body, reported in October 2022 widespread sexual violence by Ethiopian and Eritrean forces in Tigray. It also documented rapes of women and girls as young as 11 by Tigrayan forces in Amhara villages. The BBC reported in February 2021 that 200 girls under 18 had registered at health facilities in Mekelle, Tigray's capital, as rape survivors. These reports do not say how many of the girls were attacked by Eritrean soldiers.

Inside Eritrea almost nothing reaches the international counts. NCMEC, the US centre that receives online abuse reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 11 reports for Eritrea in 2024. Walk Free, an anti-slavery group, estimates 90.3 people per 1,000 in modern slavery, 320,000 in all, counting all ages and all forms. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime rates the role of criminals inside the state at 9.5 out of 10, and the US State Department places Eritrea in Tier 3, its lowest grade.

The map records no prosecution of Eritrean soldiers for abuse in Tigray and no case from inside Eritrea.

GEO.story:
The documented form of child abuse in Georgia is the making of abuse images of children to order for buyers abroad. In 2019 Georgian police, working with Australian and US authorities and Europol, the European Union's police agency, arrested 11 people and charged them. They included the owners of a photo studio and American and Australian citizens, who arranged for sexual images of girls aged 8 to 14 to be made in rented apartments in Tbilisi. Some of the girls were abused with their parents' consent, in return for 500 to 3,000 lari (about €150 to €900).

Georgia was also among the countries involved in the 2025 police operation against Kidflix, a paid streaming site for abuse videos with 1.8 million users, which led to 79 arrests across 38 countries.

NCMEC, the US centre that receives online abuse reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 17,659 reports for Georgia in 2024, or 463.2 per 100,000 people. The US State Department rates Georgia Tier 1, meaning it meets the minimum US standards against trafficking.

The Tbilisi studio is the only network on the map that produced material inside Georgia. How common paid production is there is not known.

GTM.story:
The largest part of Guatemala's record is the sale of children for adoption abroad, and state bodies took part in it. A 2009 study by the Peace Archives, an office of the presidency's Peace Secretariat, reviewed 333 of 670 adoption files from 1977 to 1989, during the civil war. It found that the army and National Police brought children into the adoption system, and that courts often declared children abandoned with little effort to find their parents. A 1977 decree let notaries, private lawyers with public powers, complete adoptions without a judge.

After the war ended in 1996 the same notary system grew into a trade. Notaries handled about 98 percent of adoptions without court review, charging $35,000 or more per child; 97 percent of the children went to the United States. In August 2007 police found 46 children up to three years old at the Casa Quivira adoption home in Antigua, most without proper documents; the attorney general investigated whether they had been stolen or taken from mothers under pressure. Guatemala passed a new adoption law in December 2007 and stopped new adoptions to the United States from 2008. In 2010 CICIG, a UN-backed commission against impunity, found that 78 percent of 153 adoptions it studied broke the law.

Children in state care were abused while officials ignored warnings. About 700 children lived at Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción, a state home built for 500; most had committed no crime. In 2016 the human rights ombudsman reported a trafficking network recruiting children there, and girls alleged sexual abuse by staff. In March 2017 police locked a group of girls in a room after an escape, and a fire killed 41 of them. In 2025 a judge convicted six former officials; the former welfare secretary received 25 years.

Guatemalan girls are also sold for sex at home and abroad. The 2025 US State Department report says gangs exploit girls in Guatemalan cities and that Guatemalan children are exploited in Mexico, the United States, Belize and El Salvador and in live-streamed abuse. In December 2024 Guatemalan authorities removed 160 children from the compound of Lev Tahor, an ultra-Orthodox sect that had moved there from Canada, following complaints of abuse and trafficking.

Adoptions abroad have stopped and the officials responsible for the 2017 fire have been convicted. Gang-run sexual exploitation of girls continues, according to the 2025 US report.

JEY.story:
Jersey's record concerns children in the island's public care. The Independent Jersey Care Inquiry heard from about 450 people connected with Jersey's care system since 1945 and reported in July 2017. It found that the States of Jersey, the island's government, had been "an ineffectual and neglectful substitute parent", that its child-welfare law was decades behind, and that some children in care might still be at risk. Haut de la Garenne, a children's home that was the centre of the police investigation Operation Rectangle from 2007 to 2010, was described by the inquiry as a symbol of these failures, and it recommended that the buildings be demolished.

The inquiry explained the failures partly by how the island was run. It found that the authorities had not made their work open to scrutiny, which fed public belief in collusion and cover-up, and that what it called a "small island culture" had gone unchallenged. Chief Minister Ian Gorst apologised, saying: "We failed children who needed our care."

NCMEC, the US centre that receives online abuse reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 325 reports for Jersey in 2024.

The inquiry warned in 2017 that some children in care might still be at risk. The map holds no later finding on whether that changed.

KWT.story:
The map holds no documented network of child abuse or trafficking in Kuwait. The one recorded event is regulatory. On 21 August 2025 Kuwait's telecoms regulator temporarily blocked Roblox, an online game platform, after parents and community groups raised concerns about children's safety on it; Qatar and Turkey had blocked it earlier that month.

The figures that exist come from outside. NCMEC, the US centre that receives online abuse reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 28,017 reports for Kuwait in 2024, or 572.1 per 100,000 people. Childlight, a research centre on child abuse data, found in 2026 that the Middle East and North Africa had no representative survey data on online sexual exploitation of children. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime rates Kuwait's human trafficking market at 8 out of 10, and Walk Free, an anti-slavery group, estimates 55,000 people in modern slavery, counting all ages and all forms.

What lies behind the online reports, and whether children are among the people trafficked, is not documented here.

MNG.story:
The record for Mongolia rests on the US State Department's 2025 trafficking report. It says women and girls are sold for sex in hotels, massage parlours, illegal brothels, bars and karaoke clubs, mostly in the capital Ulaanbaatar, in provincial centres and in border areas. Weak police enforcement sometimes makes this possible, and some families are complicit. Traffickers also use online platforms to groom children and then blackmail them. Children taken abroad for competitions have instead been put to work, for example as horse jockeys.

NCMEC, the US centre that receives online abuse reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 7,104 reports for Mongolia in 2024, or 201.5 per 100,000 people. The US State Department rates Mongolia Tier 2, meaning it does not meet the minimum US standards but is making significant efforts.

No prosecution or inquiry in Mongolia is on the map, so who runs these businesses and who pays is not documented.

IND.story:
The largest documented form of child sexual exploitation in India is the sale of girls into brothels, supplied from poor villages inside India and from Nepal and Bangladesh. Girls from other Indian states were brought to Mumbai's largest red-light district, some as young as 11, on promises of domestic work. Nepal's National Human Rights Commission estimated that 5,000 Nepali children were trafficked in 2018 and that nearly 1,000 Nepali women and girls are rescued from India each year. The 2025 US State Department reports say traffickers bribe some Indian officials, and that children are an estimated 40 percent of Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims abroad, India among the destinations.

A second form is rooted in religious custom. Girls, mostly from Dalit families, at the bottom of the caste order, are dedicated to temple deities as devadasis and then sexually exploited although Karnataka banned the practice in 1982. The state's last survey, in 2008, counted 40,600 devadasis; NGOs and a 2018 university study counted more than 80,000.

Children are also abused in homes that private charities run with state money. In 2018 the Tata Institute of Social Sciences audited 110 children's homes for the Bihar government and reported abuse or harassment at 15 of them. At the Muzaffarpur girls' home, medical checks indicated sexual abuse of 34 girls; the district child protection officer was among the accused, and the Supreme Court moved the trial to Delhi because the accused were influential in Bihar. In 2020 the operator, Brajesh Thakur, and 18 others were convicted. In Deoria, Uttar Pradesh, police freed 24 girls in 2018 from a home that had kept running after the state withdrew its recognition and funding a year earlier.

Police did not arrest Kuldeep Singh Sengar, a state legislator in Uttar Pradesh, until a high court ordered it in 2018, and the girl's father died in police custody. Sengar was convicted in 2019 of raping her.

Some adoption agencies obtained children by purchase or kidnapping for families abroad. In 2005 ten people from Hyderabad's Tender Loving Care Home were sentenced for cheating and forgery and Andhra Pradesh barred private agencies from placing children.

NCMEC, the US centre that receives online abuse reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 1,933,900 reports for India in 2024, or 133.3 per 100,000 people.

The 2025 US reports say trafficking of girls from Nepal and Bangladesh into India continues. Outside the audited homes in Bihar, how children fare in privately run state homes has not been measured.

MDA.story:
Moldova's record is mainly that of a country from which girls and women are sold for sex abroad, and the children most exposed are those who grow up in state institutions. In the mid-2000s Moldova had 68 residential institutions for children. Children left them at 15 or 16 with about US$70 and no follow-up, and UNICEF reported research showing that institutionalised children were several times more vulnerable to trafficking than other children. The US State Department reported in 2007 that women and children were trafficked from Moldova for sexual exploitation to Russia, Turkey, Israel and the United Arab Emirates, and that 12 percent of the victims helped by the International Organization for Migration were minors. Its 2025 report says traffickers still target children in or leaving state institutions.

After the wars in the former Yugoslavia, Moldovan girls were sold into brothels there whose customers included foreign troops and officials. Human Rights Watch documented in 2002 that women and girls, mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine, were held in debt bondage in bars and brothels in Bosnia. Local police acted as owners, guards and clients, and 18 monitors of the UN International Police Task Force were sent home with none confirmed prosecuted. In Kosovo, Amnesty International reported in 2004 that the international presence after 1999 generated 80 percent of traffickers' income, with women and girls brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia through Serbia.

Recruitment increasingly takes place online. The 2025 US report says traffickers use social media and video chat to recruit children through fake job advertisements and use abuse images to groom them. Moldovan courts convicted 33 traffickers in 2024, 22 of them for sex trafficking, and a former police officer received 20 years for labour trafficking; the report still lists corruption and official complicity as significant concerns. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime rates the role of criminals inside the state at 8 out of 10.

Moldova also hosts abuse material. The Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes such material, acted on 9,941 web addresses hosted there in 2025, 3 percent of its total. NCMEC, the US centre that receives reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 11,702 reports for Moldova in 2024, or 487.1 per 100,000 people.

Children leaving institutions remain the group traffickers target, according to the 2025 US report. The map has no figure for how many are trafficked each year.

NOR.story:
Norway's record centres on its role as a country that received children adopted from abroad, and on how its state kept approving those adoptions. Norway took in 6,295 children from South Korea between 1955 and 2008, and in 1974–75 Scandinavian diplomats pressed South Korea to keep sending children after it tried to stop. South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that agencies there sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand and registered children with known parents as orphans.

A Norwegian government committee, appointed in 2023, examined adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s and presented its official report, NOU 2026:7, on 22 June 2026. It found illegal or unethical conditions and clear shortcomings in the Norwegian adoption system throughout the period. Its findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would be paid if she consented, deliberately falsified documents, and payments to orphanages or organisations sometimes linked to the number of children sent. Norwegian adoption organisations did not always tell the authorities about payments or errors, and the authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegal acts. In September 2025 a Korean-born adoptee gave notice of a lawsuit against the state alleging her adoption was illegal.

Children placed in Norway's own care were also harmed. An earlier official report, NOU 2004:23, found neglect and abuse, including sexual abuse, in municipal children's homes and state special schools between 1945 and 1980. Bergen and other municipalities set up their own investigations and compensation, and in 2005 a committee of the Storting, the parliament, recommended state payments of up to NOK 300,000 with a lower burden of proof.

Norwegian police also pursue people who pay for online abuse. A method for tracing cryptocurrency payments, developed by Norwegian police in 2025, led in 2026 to the arrest of 28 men in seven countries and identified two sellers. Norway also took part in the European operations against Kidflix, a paid streaming site, and against The Com, an online network involved in sexual extortion of children. NCMEC, the US centre that receives reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 13,880 reports for Norway in 2024, or 249.1 per 100,000 people.

The 2026 report found failures across the whole period of Norway's adoptions from abroad. How many of the adopted children were taken illegally has not been counted.

PHL.story:
Most of the Philippine record is the sexual exploitation of children for money paid by men from abroad. In tourist towns children are sold in bars, brothels and on the street. When Manila's mayor Alfredo Lim closed the Ermita sex-industry district from 1992, many of its businesses moved to Angeles City and served sex tourists. The 2025 US State Department report names Angeles City, Boracay, Olongapo, Puerto Galera and Surigao, and says many foreign offenders are already convicted or charged sex offenders at home, most often in Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Britain and the United States.

In the other main setting a parent, relative or neighbour abuses a child at home on a webcam while a buyer abroad pays and gives directions. It grew while exploitation in bars fell: International Justice Mission (IJM), a US-based anti-trafficking charity, measured a fall of 79 to 86 percent in child sex trafficking in establishments in its target cities from 2006 to 2016, while Philippine internet addresses used for child exploitation each month rose more than twelvefold from 2014 to 2017. IJM estimates that 1 in 100 Filipino children was a victim of online sexual exploitation in 2022.

Because buyers and payments are abroad, cases usually start abroad. In 2017, 64 percent of cases taken up by the police anti-trafficking unit began with a foreign referral. A tip from Dutch police led to the Australian Peter Scully, who moved to Mindanao in 2011, sold videos of abuse to foreign customers and was sentenced to life in 2018. Australia's financial intelligence agency alleged that the bank Westpac had failed to check transfers linked to possible child exploitation; Westpac agreed to an A$1.3 billion penalty in 2020.

A religious leader with political ties stayed out of Philippine courts for years. Apollo Quiboloy, head of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ church and close to former president Rodrigo Duterte, was indicted in the United States in 2021 on charges including sex trafficking of children, He refused to cooperate with Philippine inquiries until he surrendered in 2024 on Philippine sexual abuse charges, which he denies. Catholic bishops said in 2002 that about 200 of 7,000 priests had committed sexual misconduct over two decades; there has been no national inquiry.

NCMEC, the US centre that receives online abuse reports, logged 1,069,705 reports for the Philippines in 2024, or 923.4 per 100,000 people.

Exploitation in bars has fallen and exploitation in homes continues. The 2025 US report still lists corruption and official complicity as significant concerns.

QAT.story:
The map holds no documented network of child abuse or trafficking based in Qatar. The recorded action is regulatory. On 13 August 2025 Qatar blocked access to Roblox, an online game platform, after parents and community groups raised concerns about children's safety on it; Kuwait and Turkey blocked it the same month.

Reports from outside suggest a large volume of online abuse that is not explained by any case on record. NCMEC, the US centre that receives online abuse reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 23,367 reports for Qatar in 2024, or 817.7 per 100,000 people. Childlight, a research centre on child abuse data, found in 2026 that the Middle East and North Africa had no representative survey data on online sexual exploitation of children. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime rates Qatar's human trafficking market at 8 out of 10, and Walk Free, an anti-slavery group, estimates 20,000 people in modern slavery, counting all ages and all forms.

What lies behind the online reports, and how many children are among those trafficked, is not documented here.

SLV.story:
The largest part of El Salvador's record is the taking of children by the armed forces during the civil war of 1980 to 1992. Pro-Búsqueda, a Salvadoran organisation founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children who disappeared during the war, most of them taken by the armed forces. Many were then adopted abroad, to the United States, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands, through flawed procedures.

The state's response has been slow. In 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, the regional human rights court, ruled on the disappearance of two sisters during a military operation in 1982. In 2010 El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children. The armed forces have still not opened their archives on the disappeared children, despite years of requests.

The current record concerns tourism. The 2025 US State Department report says foreign tourists sexually exploit children in El Salvador and that the rapid growth of tourism has created new risks. It also estimates that 140,000 to 200,000 Salvadoran children have a parent abroad or in detention. NCMEC, the US centre that receives online abuse reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 37,302 reports for El Salvador in 2024, or 588.5 per 100,000 people. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime rates the role of criminals inside the state at 7.5 out of 10.

The armed forces' archives on the children taken in the war remain closed. No case of tourist exploitation is documented on the map in detail.

VEN.story:
Most of Venezuela's record concerns girls and women who left the country during its crisis and were sold for sex in neighbouring countries. The 2025 US State Department report on Colombia says displaced Venezuelan women and girls are exploited in sex trafficking and recruited into "webcam modelling", an industry it estimates is worth over $1.2 billion a year. The report on Trinidad and Tobago says sex-trafficking victims there are mainly women and girls from Venezuela, Colombia, the Dominican Republic and Guyana, and that NGOs allege officials help with their transport and entry.

A Venezuelan criminal group controls much of this trade. Tren de Aragua, which began in Venezuela, runs sex-trafficking networks in Colombia, in Villa del Rosario and in Bogotá, Cali, Medellín and Pereira, and uses the transport hub of Cúcuta to move victims on to Argentina, Ecuador and Peru. It controls victims through pagadiarios, lodgings paid by the day that keep them in debt. In Colombia two officials who helped traffickers received plea-deal sentences of 7.5 years, below the legal minimum.

Inside Venezuela the map records abuse by Catholic priests. A 2022 Washington Post investigation found at least 10 priests accused or convicted of sexual abuse between 2001 and 2022, with complaints in at least eleven states; three served little or no sentence and returned to the priesthood. The church confirmed the report was accurate and announced an investigation.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime rates the role of criminals inside the Venezuelan state at 9 out of 10 and its resilience to organised crime at 1.88, and the US State Department places Venezuela in Tier 3, its lowest grade. NCMEC, the US centre that receives online abuse reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 74,927 reports for Venezuela in 2024, or 263.8 per 100,000 people.

The 2025 US reports describe trafficking of Venezuelan girls abroad as ongoing. The result of the church's investigation is not on record.

SYR.story:
Syria's record is dominated by sexual violence and abduction carried out during the war, by government forces and by armed groups. The UN-appointed Commission of Inquiry on Syria based its 2018 report on 454 interviews covering March 2011 to December 2017. It found that most parties committed sexual violence: women and girls were raped in detention, at checkpoints and in house raids, and male detainees, including boys, were sexually tortured. It named government forces and allied militias as the worst offenders and found the acts amounted to war crimes.

The Islamic State group (ISIS) turned the sale of girls into an organised system. After it attacked Sinjar, in Iraq, on 3 August 2014, it moved captured Yazidis, a religious minority, through holding sites in Tal Afar and Mosul, and sent women and girls on to Raqqa in Syria. Girls as young as nine were sold at market and held as sexual slaves. The commission found in June 2016 that ISIS had committed genocide; over 3,200 Yazidi women and children were then still held, mostly in Syria. ISIS also forced Syrian girls to marry its fighters. Abductions continue on a smaller recorded scale: the UN verified 14 children abducted in 2024, nine by the Patriotic Revolutionary Youth Movement, an armed youth group, four by government forces and one by the Kurdish-led YPG/YPJ, often to recruit them.

Girls who fled the war are exploited in neighbouring countries. Criminal groups recruit Syrian women and girls in Lebanon with false job offers and hold them in brothels. In 2016 Lebanese security forces freed as many as 75 Syrian women from two brothels in Jounieh; one of them had been raided in 2011, when a 17-year-old Syrian girl was found there, and reopened after about three months. In Türkiye and Jordan, the 2025 US State Department reports say Syrian refugee girls are sold or forced into marriages, and in Türkiye then held in domestic servitude and sex trafficking.

Syria is also named in a 2023 independent report for SOS Children's Villages, a charity that runs children's homes, which confirmed serious abuse allegations and cover-ups in several of its national branches.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime rates the role of criminals inside the Syrian state at 10 out of 10. NCMEC, the US centre that receives online abuse reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 32,658 reports for Syria in 2024.

Thousands of Yazidi women and children remain missing. The UN was still verifying abductions of Syrian children in 2024.

TUR.story:
The largest documented form of child exploitation in Türkiye concerns Syrian refugee girls. Türkiye hosted about 2.9 million displaced Syrians, and the 2025 US State Department report says Syrian girls, especially in poor rural regions, are forced into marriages in unofficial religious ceremonies and then held in domestic servitude and sex trafficking. The report says no investigations of complicit officials were reported, although corruption and complicity remained significant concerns. Earlier, the US State Department reported in 2007 that women and children from Moldova were trafficked to Türkiye for sexual exploitation.

Inside Türkiye, the institutional record concerns student housing. In 2016 a teacher in Karaman was arrested for abusing 10 children in student houses, two of them owned by the Ensar Foundation. The Grand National Assembly, the parliament, unanimously set up a research commission on child abuse on 24 March 2016. By July its only field visit had been to Karaman, where the provincial family directorate gave members a report blaming the victims' families. Its draft report in October 2016 recommended that the Education Ministry license and inspect student dormitories, background checks for people working with children and a wider legal definition of sexual abuse. Opposition members said the commission had not visited state nurseries, prisons or Syrian camps.

An allegation linking Türkiye to Jeffrey Epstein, the US financier who abused and trafficked girls, is under review. In December 2025 Ankara prosecutors reportedly opened an inquiry after an opposition MP, Turhan Çömez, cited US Justice Department files. The underlying document is a 2009 civil complaint alleging, "upon information and belief", that Epstein brought minor girls from Turkey and other countries; no findings or charges have been reported.

NCMEC, the US centre that receives online abuse reports mostly from US internet companies, logged 221,691 reports for Türkiye in 2024, or 259.2 per 100,000 people. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime rates the role of criminals inside the state at 9 out of 10.
